text: This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 4 Drivers of Response Risk Drivers of response risk are actions by adversarial and partner countries, firms, and individuals, potentially increasing costs or introducing vulnerabilities to DOW energy assets and operations. More broadly, adversarial actions can undermine U.S. leadership and challenge its strategic partnerships. Some single actions can lead to a variety of negative consequences, while multiple actions can compound a given consequence. 4.1 Adversary Activity in the Commercial Market China’s proactive research and commercial competition in advanced energy markets and supply chains, especially in the Li-ion battery, inverter, and PV markets, have resulted in a dominant global market position for China-based firms, bringing risks for DOW in the following areas. 4.1.1 Supply Chains The United States, and therefore DOW, is dependent on Chinese-based firms for advanced energy supplies including critical materials, components, and products, introducing longer lead times for acquisition and maintenance, cost uncertainty, and vulnerabilities to disruption due to conflicts, extreme weather, or trade factors. Moreover, China’s dominant market influence impacts the availability and cost of innovative technologies for DOW. China currently dominates the midstream supply chains (i.e., from material refining to component production) for both crystalline silicon solar PV and Li-ion batteries. In 2023, more than 90% of global polysilicon production for PV and 99% of the spherical graphite used in most Li-ion anodes was manufactured in China (Solar Media Limited/PV-Tech Research 2025; IEA 2024b). China is also home to the world’s top 10 suppliers of PV manufacturing equipment (IEA 2024c). Appendix H provides additional details on China’s dominance in the Li-ion battery supply chain. Additionally, Chinese companies have employed tactics to limit U.S. efforts to build a competitively viable domestic mining and production sector. For example, when the United States aimed to tap into its domestic lithium reserves, Chinese refiners, which control roughly two-thirds of global lithium processing, drove prices down by around 80% using strategies such as dumping and overproduction. The U.S. Defense Industrial Base is not a sufficiently large consumer of critical minerals to sustain an independent, parallel supply chain outside of China (Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party 2025). Alternative suppliers are few, and production in U.S. partner countries is often directed locally before exporting to the United States (Dollar et al. 2023). Working with other stakeholders to invest in domestic production, from mining to components, would help counter this risk. Beyond component dependence, mission owners must also grapple with cybersecurity risks embedded in a complex supply chain ecosystem, including nondefense, third-party-owned devices, where blurred responsibility for incident response complicates risk management and mission assurance. For instance, it is difficult to determine who is responsible for cybersecurity incident response if nation-state adversaries compromise residential rooftop solar inverters, which may be aggregated by a third-party overseas company providing grid stability services through a power purchase agreement with a local utility. Improving cybersecurity in DOW and power provider networks could mitigate this risk. 13 This report is available at no cost
